question: Is a new convert sinful for not wearing hijab out of fear of her family and society?
asked: She is a convert in Austria who has not told anyone in her family about her conversion and is worried about their reaction. She is not wearing the hijab because of the repercussions it would bring, and not wearing it causes her so much stress that she is crying and fearful of Jahannam and of Allah's punishment. She thinks her conversion is pointless and will not be accepted because she does not dress with the hijab.
answer:
Dearest sister in Islam, alhamdulillah, thumma alhamdulillah, Allah 'azza wa jall has guided you to Islam. Allah has blessed you with the kalimah. Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has chosen you out of billions and billions of people to be guided to this faith, in a land where Muslims are very, very few in number, a small percentage, and in a land where Islamophobia is on the rise. Austria is the land where Hitler came from, and the neo-Nazis are on the rise there, and the parliament is trying to enact things that are very Islamophobic.

By the way, most of you are probably not aware of this, but Austria is one of the most Islamophobic places in terms of the government. Obviously the people are the people, but in terms of the government, it is very, very difficult over there, probably just one notch less than France. France, as we know, in terms of Europe and the Western world, has no competition; France is in its own category. It has waged war against the outer symbols of Islam, and against the religion of Islam, and therefore against practicing Muslims. Right after that would be, in my humble opinion, Austria. And I could be wrong in that specific analysis, but Austria is Islamophobic by and large. The current government is highly Islamophobic, the far-right parties are rising, and there is a lot of tension.

And in this environment, our sister, mashaAllah, tabarakAllah, Allah has guided her to Islam. But she is worried about the fact that she has kept it hidden. Now, as for the fact that it is hidden, I have a much longer Q&A where I have gone into details. No problem; you don't have to tell anybody if it's going to be problematic. Allah 'azza wa jall knows you are a Muslimah. You have said the kalimah in private, and you are, I'm assuming, practicing to the best of your level, in terms of salah and in terms of other things, whatever you're able to do without causing harm to yourself. So alhamdulillah, Allah has guided you to Islam, and that is a blessing so huge, so magnificent and so blessed that every other sin after it is trivial compared to the blessing of being upon Islam.

So realize, dear sister in Islam, that yes, indeed, modest clothing is something that we should definitely strive for, and it is part and parcel of our Shari'ah. And there is no denying that the default is that men should be covered in a specific manner, to a specific area of the body, and women as well should be covered as much as possible. Included in that is, of course, the head covering, which is called the hijab, and covering the entire body in a modest or loose manner. And this is something that really there's no difference of opinion on. However, dearest sister, the obligation is the general rule. The obligation is the general rule, and there are a number of things you need to take into account.

First and foremost, just to be technical here: indeed it is obligatory, but the obligation of the hijab, or of dressing modestly with loose clothing and whatnot, is not at the same level as the obligation of accepting Islam, which is far more important, or of salah, or of charity. There is no comparison between them. And the blessings of salah and of zakah and of siyam, and the power of these rituals to forgive all sins, is something that is well known. So do not compare apples and oranges in this regard. No doubt the hijab, and overall modest dressing for men and women, is part and parcel of our Shari'ah. But even in the Madinan phase, the rulings of the hijab came down in the fifth year of the hijrah, one of the last of the major rulings to come down. After all of the other rulings came down, then that ruling came down.

Also realize, dear sister, that the Shari'ah has come with a beautiful reality of taking our circumstances into account. You see, it is one thing to speak in general, and that's true: generally speaking, such and such is obligatory. But the Shari'ah also takes into account the specifics of your situation. And as for your situation, you know best how difficult it is. I do not know the details of your situation. Is there a genuine fear for your safety? Are you living with your parents, and if you were to publicly announce your embracing Islam and wear the hijab, they would kick you out and you might be on the streets? Or is there physical danger? If the danger is such that it is to your persona, or to your necessary livelihood, or to your basic well-being, in this case it constitutes a darurah, and the wearing of the hijab would then actually be exempted from you. So the general rule would be lifted from you, and **you are absolutely sinless in that case.**

And again, only you know best whether it is at that level or not; I cannot tell from the question. So do not make the Shari'ah more difficult. Our Lord is forgiving, and our Lord is merciful, and our Lord understands that you are a young lady who has embraced Islam in a strange land, in a foreign land. Very few Muslims are there, and the struggles for you, in terms of your livelihood, or in terms of the far right, or in terms of your parents or whatnot, might be too much for you to bear. So if that is the case, and you know best, then it would not be obligatory on you, if there is a threat to your persona, to your sanity, to your living a regular, normal life that most people live.

Now, suppose it's not at that level. Suppose it goes down a notch. Suppose that some doors might be shut but others will be open. Suppose that people will stare at you, but there's no physical danger. In this case, the default ruling would still apply, which is that it is obligatory, and you should strive your best to do it. Nonetheless, dearest sister, in case you find that this is not something that you're able to meet, and this is something that you're falling short of, then realize that this is a sin, and all of us are sinners. And the solution to sinning is not to give up hope. The solution to a sin is not to despair and just say, "Oh, Allah is never going to forgive me." The solution is to work on what you can do and increase that. And the solution is to ask Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to make what you're not doing possible for you to do, and to give you the strength and the courage to do that. And while you're in that interim, continue to do the good that you're doing.

Dearest sister, your prayer to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is infinitely more powerful and more important than your wearing the veil. And of course, wearing the veil is important; I'm not saying it's not. But increase your prayer, increase your Qur'an, increase your charity, increase the purity of your heart. And if you're not able to wear the headscarf because of the difficulties of the land, then at least try to be as modest in your clothing as possible. And if it just requires courage and fortitude, then work your way there bit by bit, incrementally. Aim for it: "Inshallah, one day I'm going to do it." And get help from other sisters; get help from local communities. There are masajid in Austria, some major masajid, as you're aware. They're thriving. They're obviously a minority in the land, just like in most Western lands, but they are there. So connect with them, and get help and tips from them about what can be done to battle the Islamophobia or the far right and whatnot.

And in the meantime, dearest sister, do not despair of Allah's mercy. Your email really was a very emotional email, that you feel your Islam is in vain. A'udhu billah, sister, you have accepted Islam, alhamdulillah, thumma alhamdulillah. You're not going to be perfect, and you have to accept that, because none of us is perfect. I'm not perfect. No human being is perfect. So if you put it in your mind that if I'm not perfect, Allah 'azza wa jall will not forgive me, that is an incorrect perception, dearest sister. Allah forgives all of us because He is the Forgiving, and Allah wants to see the effort, and Allah wants to see the sincerity, and Allah recognizes that we are all going to fall short. So do as much good as you can, seek Allah's forgiveness for what you cannot do, and continue to strive to better yourself.

Dear sister, none of us is perfect. But as long as we believe in Allah, and as long as we lower our heads to Allah, and as long as we recognize that we are sinful and there is no salvation for us other than by turning to Allah and seeking His istighfar, and we try to be better, we aim to be better, then alhamdulillah, we are upon good, and we can hope, and we should hope, and we must hope for the mercy of Allah jalla jalaluhu. So I hope that this answers your question. And once again, congratulations, mabruk for having accepted this beautiful faith, and welcome to the global brotherhood and sisterhood of the religion of Islam.
